Question: If \(P\) is the product of \(n\) quantities in geometric progression, \(S\) their sum, and \(S'\) the sum of their reciprocals, then \(P\) in terms of \(S,\) \(S',\) and \(n\) is:
Solution:
Reciprocals require nonzero terms, but the statement does not require positive terms. This matters when taking a square root and when dividing by \(S'\).

Write the nonzero real terms as \(a_j=ar^{j-1}\), for \(1\le j\le n\), where \(a\ne0\) and \(r\ne0\). Terms equally far from opposite ends have the same product:
\[
a_j a_{n+1-j}=a^2r^{n-1}=K.
\]
Here \(K\ne0\). Thus each reciprocal is the opposite term divided by \(K\), giving
\[
S'=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1{a_j}
=\frac1K\sum_{j=1}^n a_{n+1-j}
=\frac S K.
\]
Multiplying all \(n\) opposite-term identities also gives
\[
P^2=\prod_{j=1}^n(a_j a_{n+1-j})=K^n.
\]
Consequently, \(S=KS'\) and \(P^2=K^n\) hold without any assumption of positivity.

If all terms are positive, then \(S'>0\), \(K=S/S'>0\), and \(P>0\). Taking the positive square root is then justified, yielding
\[
P=\boxed{\left(\frac S{S'}\right)^{n/2}},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{B}\). For even \(n\) with \(S'\ne0\), the same formula also follows by grouping the terms into \(n/2\) opposite pairs, without needing positivity.

However, the printed conditions allow the progression \((-1,-1,-1)\). It has \(n=3\), \(S=S'=-3\), and \(P=-1\), whereas choice B gives \(1\). In fact, every listed expression is positive for this example, so none equals \(P\).

There is also a possible zero denominator: the progression \((1,-1)\) has well-defined reciprocals but \(S=S'=0\). Thus \(S/S'\) is undefined. Choice \(\mathrm{B}\) is valid under a positive-term assumption, but no listed formula is universally valid as written.
